panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Preoperative clinical photo of left hand in neutral wrist position showing severe long finger and mild ring finger flexion contracture in case report titled Localized type Volkmann's contracture; classic Volkmann tenodesis effect. B: Same hand different view with wrist neutral showing fixed flexion contracture of long and ring fingers consistent with localized Volkmann ischemic contracture. C: Same hand with wrist in palmar flexion demonstrating reduction of finger flexion contractures - Volkmann tenodesis sign supporting localized Volkmann ischemic contracture.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of a real patient explicitly described in the caption as a 58-year-old woman with severe Volkmann Ischemic Contracture complicated by anaerobic infection, with residual bandage traces. A claw-type hand deformity is visible; the severe infected presentation makes it atypical. Disease attribution is directly supported by the caption and the VIC-focused article title. B: Radiograph of the same patient, captioned as showing a wrist fracture and gas bubbles in the forearm soft tissue confirming gas gangrene, a described complication of the Volkmann Ischemic Contracture. It is a real human-patient image directly attributed to the target disease; the specific radiographic signs (gas bubbles, wrist fracture) are not in the allowed vocabulary, so they are listed as proposed findings.

panels.figure_caption: On the left figure it is about a 58-year-old woman with a severe case of Volkmann Ischemic Contracture complicated by an anaerobic bacteria infection; we can still see the traces of the bandage. The right picture is the same patient with an X-ray showing a wrist fracture and gas bubbles inside the soft tissue of the forearm, confirming gas gangrene.
in_text_mentions: ger of compartment syndrome or Volkmann’s contracture, which is why the urgently needed management is not provided, resulting in serious complications including anaerobic infection with gas gangrene (Figure 1), common bacterial infections, osteitis, and severe contractures characterized by necrosis of all flexor muscles and extensor muscles, which further complicates the treatment. In our series, Volkmann’s syndrome is observed in children, adolescents, and adults, resulting from fractures or soft tissue trauma (Figure 2). We must insist that a clear clinical presentation of Volkmann’s ischemi

s with common germs, and a case of osteitis in a 24-year-old man. These cases are unusual, and we have not found similar cases in the literature. Another difference is about X-rays useful for identifying displaced fractures and associated lesions (such as bubbles inside soft tissue, confirming gas gangrene as in Figure 1) or confirming osteitis secondary to infected Volkmann Ischemic Contracture. Imaging studies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) may prove to be supportive in the diagnosis of VIC [19], but they are not considered as first-line investigations.
